summary: In Greek mythology the Oneiroi (singular Oneiros) are the personified spirits of dreams. Dreams were not generally personified in ancient Greek thought, but where they were, the Oneiroi appear as a collective "tribe of Dreams" born of Nyx (Night), serving as divine messengers who carry visions from the gods to sleeping mortals. They figure most prominently in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and in Hesiod's Theogony, while Ovid's Metamorphoses later names individual dream-deities such as Morpheus, Phobetor (Icelos), and Phantasos as sons of Somnus (Sleep).
etymology: From Ancient Greek Ὄνειρος (Oneiros), "dream"; the plural Ὄνειροι (Oneiroi) denotes the collective dream-spirits.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: In Hesiod's Theogony the Oneiroi belong to the "tribe of Dreams" (phylon Oneiron) and are counted among the offspring of Nyx (Night), born without a father. Their siblings are likewise dark personifications, including Moros (Doom), Ker (Destiny), Thanatos (Death), Hypnos (Sleep), Momus (Blame), Oizys (Pain), the Keres, Nemesis, and Eris (Discord).

Ovid's Metamorphoses offers a different genealogy, assigning a thousand sons to Somnus (Sleep, the Roman counterpart of Hypnos). Among these dream-deities Ovid singles out three by name: Morpheus, Phobetor (whom the gods call Icelos), and Phantasos.

sections.heading: Dwelling and the Gates of Horn and Ivory
paragraphs: The Odyssey places a "land of dreams" beyond the streams of Oceanus, near the Asphodel Meadows where the spirits of the dead dwell. From this realm the dreams pass to the sleeping.

Homer also distinguishes true dreams from false ones by the gate through which they come: truthful dreams issue from a gate made of horn, while deceitful dreams pass through a gate made of ivory. The image of the twin gates became a lasting symbol of the reliability, or unreliability, of dreams.

sections.heading: Role as Divine Messengers
paragraphs: In the Iliad, Zeus sends a baleful dream to Agamemnon, dispatching an Oneiros to deliver false divine instructions. The dream-figure assumes the shape of Nestor, Agamemnon's trusted counselor, illustrating the capacity of the Oneiroi for shape-shifting and for impersonating those whom the dreamer trusts.

Ovid characterizes the named dream-deities by the forms they take: Morpheus appears in human shape and mimics the voices and gestures of people; Phobetor (Icelos) manifests as beasts, birds, and serpents; and Phantasos takes the form of inanimate objects such as earth, rock, water, and wood. Together they shape the visions that come to mortals in sleep.
